job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior data analyst at a freight and warehousing company in Port Ellis. I studied computer science, and my final project was a tool that predicted late deliveries for a local courier. Most days I clean up shipment data, build weekly reports in a spreadsheet and a dashboard tool, and answer questions from the operations team. I rent a one-bed flat with my partner Noah, who's a nurse on shifts. I keep a budget spreadsheet for the two of us, and I'm always a little stressed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that it's useful for certain jobs and overhyped for others. I use an AI assistant now and then to write formulas, and it's handy, but I check everything. At work I'd say we should use it for the boring parts and keep people for decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with the plateau but I'm not carefree. Port Ellis doesn't have many data jobs, and my company isn't growing fast. If my manager Dolores left, I don't know who would speak up for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd learn the cloud database tools that the warehouse team uses, since they're what gets budgets. I'd move 60 a month to savings by trimming our grocery bill, and Noah and I would keep our no-new-clothes year going. And I'd keep a copy of my best reports in a folder, in case I need to show someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little ache about money. Like a steady drizzle rather than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How tight is the household budget, and what gives first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our budget is tight. Rent is 900, my loan repayment is 190, and Noah's pay depends on how many shifts he gets. If either of us loses hours, we'd feel it in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Noah handle a money scare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk it through with Noah on a Sunday night, with the spreadsheet open. That's how we handle things. Not dramatic, but there's a plan on a page.

say: I'd say it's **useful** for some jobs and overhyped for others.
At work I'd suggest using it for **boring parts** and keeping people for decisions.
think: I'm fine with the plateau but not **carefree**, since Port Ellis has few data jobs.
If my manager Dolores left, I'm not sure who would **speak up** for me.
do: Learn the **cloud database** tools the warehouse team uses.
Move **60** a month to savings by trimming groceries.
Keep a **folder** of my best reports to show someone.
feel: I feel mostly **calm**, with a little ache about money, like steady drizzle.

fieldNote: Tara's calm comes from **planning on paper**, and her household budget is the real pressure.
Her partner Noah's shift-based income adds a second weak point.
She uses AI lightly and keeps checking the results.

steps.text: Learn the cloud database tools used by the warehouse team
Keep our no-new-clothes year going and trim groceries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to be honest about it. At work I'd tell Dolores that the reports we spend days on could be done in minutes, and that we should decide what we do with the saved time before someone decides for us. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because I don't want to sound like I'm panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is clearly in the zone. Data cleaning, reporting and answering questions are what AI does well. If the company needs one analyst instead of three, I'm a junior and it's easy to see who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to become the person who checks the AI's numbers and explains them to operations, because a reader still has to trust what they're told. I'd take a data engineering course that the firm half-pays for. And I'd quietly update my CV and start talking to the logistics people in the port, since there are other firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a manageable kind. It's like being told the road ahead will be diverted, and you know there's another way but not which one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think about my colleague Mehdi, who's in his forties and does the same thing as me with more experience. If the firm cuts, my colleague Mehdi would be kept first, and I'd be happy for him and scared for me at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner Noah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say to Noah that we need to hold off on moving to a bigger flat and on the holiday we've been planning. That's a small cost, but it's what steadiness looks like.

say: I'd tell my manager Dolores to **decide** what we do with saved time before someone decides for us.
Online I'd stay **quiet**, to avoid sounding like I'm panicking.
think: Data cleaning and reporting are exactly what AI does **well**.
If the firm needs one analyst instead of three, a **junior** goes first.
do: Become the person who **checks** the AI's numbers and explains them to operations.
Take a **data engineering** course the firm half-pays for.
Quietly update my **CV** and talk to other port logistics firms.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but manageable, like a diverted road with another way.

fieldNote: Tara works through **role change**: become the trusted checker, keep options open, delay big purchases.

She stays quiet in public to avoid looking alarmed.

steps.text: Start checking and explaining AI-produced reports for operations
Take the half-paid data engineering course
Update my CV and contact other logistics firms at the port
Hold off the bigger flat and holiday with Noah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is nowhere near enough for anyone. At work I'd ask what the plan is, and the honest answer would be that nobody has one. Online I wouldn't say much, because there's nothing to say that doesn't sound like panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's frightening. My whole field is the first thing in line, and the entry-level data jobs are probably gone in 18 months. Noah's nursing is safer for a while, which helps, but I'd be a household of one income and a lot of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut our spending to the bone, move out of the one-bed into a room in a shared house, and push savings to about 500 a month by selling things. I'd move toward something that touches the physical world, like logistics operations on the warehouse floor, where robots take longer. And I'd look at nursing support or technical roles at the hospital where Noah works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steady kind. I'd get really organised. Panicking doesn't pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which plans would you have to give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd miss is the plan we'd made. We wanted to save for a deposit in three years, and my partner Noah wants a baby at some point. I'd put those on hold, and that's the real loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also lean on my sister Imani, who lives two hours away. She has a spare room and a small garden. We'd be down to the basics, but we'd manage.

say: I'd say two years is **nowhere near enough**, and ask what the plan is.
Online I'd say little, because anything honest sounds like **panic**.
think: My field is first in line, and entry-level data jobs may vanish in **18 months**.
Noah's nursing is **safer**, but I'd be one income with a lot of rent.
do: Cut spending to the bone and move into a **shared house**.
Push savings to about **500** a month by selling things.
Look for **warehouse floor** or hospital technical roles that robots reach later.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but steady, because panicking doesn't pay the bills.
S2.quote: We wanted to save for a deposit in three years, and my partner Noah wants a baby at some point.
fieldNote: Tara's fear is **organised**: cut costs, find physical-world work, and use her sister's spare room.
The real loss is the deposit and Noah's wish for a baby, so the household's plans are the first casualty.
She expects her field to go first but relies on Noah's steadier nursing income.

steps.text: Move from the one-bed to a room in a shared house
Save about 500 a month by selling things
Apply for warehouse operations and hospital technical jobs
Ask my sister Imani for her spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to take seriously and short enough to start now. I'd suggest at work that we map which roles change first and retrain people before the cuts. Online I might share articles, but I'd keep it low-key.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say it's a window. By 2031 I'd be 27, with a few years of savings and a chance to move into something less exposed. But I'd also worry the window is smaller than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a qualification in operations or supply chain management, since it combines data with the real world. I'd save 150 a month, and I'd try to put the loan down by a quarter. I'd also stay close to Dolores and ask her to take me on bigger projects, so I'm hard to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in a cautious way. Like having a long exam and a few months to revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go wrong if five years turned out to be three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it turned out that five was really three, I'd be caught halfway through my course. That's the risk, so I'd look for a course that gives a certificate each term, so I'm never left with a half-finished thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah about the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Noah about the baby plan and say that we should aim to decide in two years, not now. That keeps the option open.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to take **seriously** and short enough to start now.
At work I'd suggest mapping which roles change **first** and retraining before cuts.
think: I'd see a **window**, since at 27 I'd have savings and a chance to move.
The window may be **smaller** than people think.
do: Study part-time for **supply chain** or operations, mixing data with the real world.

feel: I feel **cautiously hopeful**, like a long exam with a few months to revise.
S3.quote: I'd look for a course that gives a certificate each term, so I'm never left with a half-finished thing.
fieldNote: Tara handles uncertainty by choosing **stackable credentials**, which protect her if the date slips.
She treats the baby decision as something to set a date for rather than avoid.
Her mood stays anxious because the entry-level data job is still the exposed one.

steps.text: Study part-time for a supply chain or operations qualification
Save 150 a month and cut the loan by a quarter
Ask Dolores for bigger projects to become harder to cut
Decide with Noah about a baby in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time for a proper plan, and I'd say so. I'd suggest at work that we invest in people, not only tools. I'd tell friends that the answer is to learn and adapt, as sensible as that sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32 by 2036. My honest view is that I'd have a decent chance of being fine, with a mortgage, a partner and a career that's changed shape. I wouldn't be carefree, but I'd feel I have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move up from analyst to operations or product, where knowing the business counts. I'd save for a deposit and keep our spending steady. And I'd take one new AI tool each year and see whether it fits my work, because I'm the kind of person who waits until it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A bit like looking at a long hill from the bottom: tiring, but you can see the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you after a decade of notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would worry me is whether the pay keeps up. If the work is there but the pay isn't, a mortgage becomes a trap. I'd watch what the unions and the government are saying about pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to bet, what does your life look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to bet, we'd have a flat, a baby and a smaller holiday. Not a bad outcome at all, honestly.

say: I'd say ten years is time for a **proper plan**, and we should invest in people, not only tools.
I'd tell friends to **learn and adapt**, sensible as that sounds.
think: At 32 I'd have a decent chance of being **fine**, with a changed career.
I'd not be carefree, but I'd feel I have **time**.
do: Move from analyst to **operations** or product, where business knowledge counts.
Save for a **deposit** and keep spending steady.
Try one **new AI tool** a year once it's proven.
feel: I feel **fairly calm**, like looking up a long hill from the bottom.
S4.quote: If the work is there but the pay isn't, a mortgage becomes a trap.
fieldNote: Tara plans a **steady career climb** and tests one AI tool a year, matching her wait-until-proven style.
Her remaining concern is pay and hours, not jobs existing.
She describes a modest, believable future: flat, baby and a smaller holiday.

steps.text: Move from analyst to an operations or product role
Save a deposit while keeping spending steady
Test one proven AI tool each year
Plan for a baby with Noah once the flat is secured

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything in my field goes at once, and we'd have one income and rent. What would help is a retraining scheme with a stipend, a warning from my firm, and my sister's spare room if it came to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not the dramatic type, so I'd probably sound fine when I'm not. If you take my words at face value, you'll miss how much I'm putting in the budget to stay ahead.

headlineQuote: I'm not the dramatic type, so I'd probably sound fine when I'm not.
portrait: Tara is a **junior data analyst** at a freight firm, renting a one-bed with her partner Noah, a nurse on shifts.
She's **steady**: uses AI now and then, checks it, and plans on paper with a budget spreadsheet.
Her worry is the **entry-level** data job disappearing while rent and Noah's shift pay stay tight.
Her plans are practical: stackable **qualifications**, savings and hands-on work as backup.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because her whole field goes first and the household has little cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining scheme with a **stipend**, early warning from her firm and her sister's spare room.
